Playing RPGs. By myself. As in table-top, or a sort of tabletop-computer hybrid.

There are others who do it, and even a few systems for it, but I'm pretty sure you'd get looked at weird if you told almost anyone about it. Some people even rant about it not being role playing as though it were a religious issue, believe it or not.

I believe there are two rationales to this.

The first, most common one, and the one most loudly repeated, is that it isn't RP because RP requires two or more people. Someone to put it into context, perhaps, or someone to participate with. Obviously I disagree with this. I think some may also make the case that it requires input from other people, which is in most of these solo rule sets provided by some kind of randomization system, e.g. charts with varying levels of probability, randomizers, etc., which work together with the player's imagination to provide input from another source.

The second is more subtle and a lot more gray, in that it isn't RP because it's creative writing. There is some truth to this - most people use a computer in it (for most, the experience is made "concrete" by somehow doing something with it, and typing it into a computer as it happens is how most people do it). Plus, the biggest solo RP tool out there (Mythic) states that it can be used as a writing tool. That said, IMO it can easily be both, and arguably a lot of creative writing is arguably RP to one degree or another.
I admit that comes off as a little creepy.
I've played a lot of tabletop before but this is the first I've heard of solo play. How does it work? Can you provide me any resources for getting started?

Certainly!

Solo RP (or solitaire RP, as it is often called - "solo" also refers to one-on-one player/GM RP) does have some requirements before you play. The first and foremost is that you have a good imagination, because you're going to need to rapidly come up with stuff from words. Second, you're going to need patience, because this does not always come right away, and you're going to need practice.

I will use Mythic as an example. Mythic is probably the 800 pound gorilla in this category, and for good reason - it's a highly-generalized and adaptable game system. It refers to itself as a "GM Emulator," and most solo systems use some sort of GM emulation capability.

When you want to do something, you generally "ask" the emulator about it. It is phrased as a yes/no question, with the possibility of "extreme yes" and "extreme no." The chart works in one of two ways. When you are asking a general question, you use your assessment of the likelihood of a yes to determine the row of the chart to use, and what is called the "chaos level" to determine the column. The combination yields cell that contains a roll-under number for the result, along with criteria for an exceptional yes or no. You then roll it to determine the outcome. You can also use two characters' stats, translated into the Mythic probability assessment system, to determine the column/row to use, and can use it to arbitrate, say, combat.

There is usually more to it than that, though. In Mythic, the chaos level is a more complicated mechanic - essentially you move it up for more 'chaos' and down for less 'chaos.' This does not just control the column in the chart. On certain rolls, you also get a random event, where you roll against a chart to get some words, and use these to construct an outcome.

For instance, let's say I'm playing the character Jim. I "ask" the system, "Is the door locked?" I think it's Very Likely and my chaos level for the scene is 5 (average). I look this up on the table, and the cell I get gives me a 70 (out of 100) as a roll-under-or-equal number. I roll a 1d100 and get 44, under 70, so the GM Emulator answered "yes." However, because of the chaos level rules, that 44 triggered a random event. I roll against the tables, and get "NPC Action," "Attack", and "Structure." So I interpret that to mean that I am not alone and someone ELSE is trying to break into the building at the same time. But I could also have had the structure have automated defenses attacking me. Or I could have had a conflict going on inside the structure. Or something else. You go from that. Note that not all questions have a random event - most don't, in fact, I just threw that in as an example. There are a number of other rules, such as how to initiate scenes and ask more complex questions, and guidelines on how to integrate other rulesets (e.g. D&D) into it.

There are several different engines in use. A free one is CRGE - the [Conjectural Roleplaying GM Emulator] (http://www.drivethrurpg.com/product/145426/CRGE-Conjectural-Roleplaying-GM-Emulator). I don't have a lot of familiarity with it, but it doesn't seem as flexible as Mythic. Another one that is not free is the Covetous Poet's Adventure Creator and Solo GM Guidebook. This is well thought-out system, but the solo mode focuses on putting you in the GM chair, not the player chair.

There are also simpler solo systems. Perhaps the simplest is to roll a 1d6, but that doesn't have a whole lot of spice to it. A more sophisticated version of this is available at Tiny Solitary Soldiers. Someone made a Fate add-on for solo RP which is a bit simpler than Mythic, but it gives a bit of an idea of what it's like.

It is also part of other systems, such as Scarlet Heroes, Tunnels and Trolls, and Traveler. I know very little about these systems, but the latter two seem to be popular. If solitaire rules aren't included, then they're at least used a lot by the solo RP community, such as it is.

There are some caveats you have to be aware of when working with these things. It is NOT like regular role-playing with others. It's a lot closer to Internet role-playing. This is fine for me but others have varying levels of compatability with it. It requires, as I said, creativity and patience. You often need to make it concrete in one way or another, which many people do with writing out the adventure. You also have to learn what the best line is for GM and player - although you're using the GM emulator, you ultimately have final authority, and you need to know when to override it, since you can't just follow it blindly. This is something that is fine tuned over some play, though. NPCs are also difficult to handle - there are various approaches, and I think some people are trying to work out better systems, but for now it can be pretty imperfect to have a lot of party members that would normally be played by others.

Here are some sites that might interest you:

http://soloroleplayer.com/solo-rpg-resources-tools/ - A listing of a lot of other resources on the topic.

http://thelonecrusader.com/ - A blog focusing on solitaire Dungeons and Dragons.

https://boardgamegeek.com/guild/1999 - A forum devoted to this topic.

https://solorpgvoyages.wordpress.com/ - A blog devoted to the topic, and also reviews various GM emulation systems.

https://plus.google.com/communities/116965157741523529510 - A Google group dedicated to this topic.

There are also groups on Yahoo, such as a Mythic fan group, and a lot of forums/sub-forums. There are also a lot of examples of various play sessions with Mythic, which ought to be of help, and will describe its actual use better than I can.

Hopefully that's enough to start you out. If not, let me know and I'll see if I can root around some more for you.
